title: Self-Inductance
short_intro: Self-inductance is the property of a single electrical conductor or coil by which a change in electric current flowing through it induces an electromotive force (EMF) in the same conductor. This phenomenon is a direct consequence of Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and Lenz's law.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of self-inductance, magnetic flux linkage, formula L = Nphi/I, self-inductance of a long straight solenoid, simple numericals on inductance, and qualitative understanding of back-EMF.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed field-theoretic derivations of self-inductance for coaxial cables and toroids, stored magnetic energy density, transient growth and decay of current in LR circuits, and coupling with AC impedance phenomena.

prerequisites: Lenz's law and direction of induced EMF
Ampere's circuital law and magnetic field of solenoids

concept_notes.heading: Origin and Definition of Self-Inductance
bullets: When an electric current I passes through a coil of N turns, it produces a magnetic flux phi through each turn.
The total magnetic flux linkage (Nphi) is directly proportional to the current I flowing through the coil, provided the magnetic permeability of the medium remains constant.
Mathematically expressed as Nphi = L I, where L is the coefficient of self-induction or simply self-inductance.

concept_notes.heading: Back-EMF and Lenz's Law Interpretation
bullets: Any change in current (dI/dt) causes a change in magnetic flux linkage, inducing an electromotive force e given by e = - d(Nphi)/dt = - L (dI/dt).
The negative sign embodies Lenz's law, signifying that the induced EMF opposes the change in current that produces it.
For a growing current, the induced EMF acts in the opposite direction to the applied voltage, while for a decaying current, it acts in the same direction to maintain the current.

concept_notes.heading: Dimensions and SI Units
bullets: The SI unit of self-inductance is the henry (H), equivalent to volt-second per ampere (V·s/A) or ohm-second.
The dimensional formula of self-inductance is [M L^2 T^{-2} A^{-2}].
An inductor of 1 henry induces a back-EMF of 1 volt when the current changes at the rate of 1 ampere per second.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Energy Stored in an Inductor
bullets: Work must be done by an external source to establish current against the opposing back-EMF in an inductor.
This instantaneous work is stored within the magnetic field of the inductor as potential energy.
The total energy stored when a current I is established is given by U = (1/2) L I^2.

derivations.title: Self-Inductance of a Long Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Long air-cored solenoid of length l, cross-sectional area A, total turns N, and uniform turn density n = N/l.
steps: Write the magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid carrying current I: B = mu_0 n I = mu_0 (N/l) I.
Calculate the magnetic flux through a single turn of the solenoid: phi = B A = (mu_0 N I A) / l.
Multiply by the total number of turns N to get the total flux linkage: Nphi = N [(mu_0 N I A) / l] = (mu_0 N^2 A / l) I.
Compare with the defining relation Nphi = L I to extract the self-inductance expression.
derivations.result: L = \frac{mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = mu_0 n^2 A l

derivations.title: Energy Stored in an Inductor
derivations.conditions: Inductor of self-inductance L carrying a time-varying current i(t).
steps: Express the instantaneous power delivered to the inductor to overcome back-EMF: P = -e cdot i = (L \frac{di}{dt}) i.
Express the small work done dW in time dt as dW = P dt = L i di.
Integrate the work from zero current to final current I to find total stored energy: U = int_{0}^{I} L i di.
Evaluate the integral to yield the final energy formula.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current Growth in an LR Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential growth curve of current i versus time t, asymptotically approaching the maximum value I_0 = V/R, with the tangent at t=0 intercepting the asymptote at t = L/R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how inertia of the inductor delays the instantaneous rise of current due to opposing back-EMF.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQs regarding time constant and exponential rise.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Flux vs Current Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin for linear magnetic materials, and a hysteresis/saturation curve for ferromagnetic cores.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the linear graph directly represents the constant self-inductance L of the inductor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test understanding of linearity and core saturation effects in inductors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Induced EMF vs Rate of Change of Current
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear plot of magnitude of induced EMF (|e|) versus di/dt with a positive slope equal to L.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates strict proportionality between the back-EMF and the rate of change of current.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical data interpretation in TGT/PGT problem sets.

solved_numericals.question: A coil has 500 turns and a current of 2 A produces a magnetic flux of 4 x 10^{-3} Wb through each turn. Calculate the self-inductance of the coil.
solution_steps: Identify given values: N = 500, I = 2 A, phi = 4 \times 10^{-3} Wb.
Apply the formula for magnetic flux linkage: Nphi = 500 \times 4 \times 10^{-3} = 2.0 Wb.
Use the definition L = Nphi / I.

solved_numericals.question: An inductor of inductance 5 H carries a steady current of 2 A. What is the magnetic energy stored in the inductor?
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 5 H, I = 2 A.
Recall the formula for stored magnetic energy: U = (1/2) L I^2.

solved_numericals.question: A solenoid of length 0.5 m, cross-sectional area 10 cm^2, and 1000 turns is filled with a magnetic material of relative permeability mu_r = 500. Calculate its self-inductance.
solution_steps: Convert dimensions to SI units: l = 0.5 m, A = 10 \times 10^{-4} m^2 = 10^{-3} m^2, N = 1000, mu_r = 500.
Use the formula for self-inductance with a core medium: L = (mu_r mu_0 N^2 A) / l.
Calculate final value: L = 1000 \times 4pi \times 10^{-4} = 0.4pi H approx 1.256 H.

assumptions_and_limitations: Self-inductance L is assumed to be constant, which holds true only for linear magnetic materials (mu is independent of B).
Fringing fields at the ends of finite solenoids are neglected in standard analytical formulas, requiring long solenoid approximations (l >> r).

common_misconceptions.wrong: An inductor opposes the flow of steady direct current (DC).
common_misconceptions.correct: An ideal inductor offers zero resistance and acts as a short circuit for steady DC in steady state.
common_misconceptions.why: Inductance opposes only the change in current (di/dt), not the steady current itself.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Self-inductance depends on the magnitude of current passing through the coil.
common_misconceptions.correct: Self-inductance is a purely geometric property of the conductor configuration and core material permeability.
common_misconceptions.why: In linear media, flux linkage Nphi increases proportionally with I, keeping the ratio L = Nphi / I constant.

quick_revision: Self-inductance L is defined by Nphi = L I and measured in henries (H).
Magnetic Flux Linkage Definition: Nphi = L I
Induced EMF in an Inductor: e = -L \frac{di}{dt}
